visible.summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arizona among its 'low-risk states' group: it has largely refrained from targeting transgender adults, and although it has enacted policies affecting trans youth, the map's author considers them unlikely to be extended to adults. That is the assessment's praise of restraint, not of protection — no extraordinary protective measures are recorded for Arizona.

The local scene has tracked the national chill: Tucson cancelled its historic 2026 Pride celebration, citing a political and financial environment that made hosting nearly impossible and attending potentially unsafe.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2026 Pride cancellations (Tucson) are an LGBT+-visibility conflict rather than a trans-specific measure, but they track the same climate of official hostility that shapes enforcement posture.
visible.localsOnly: Arizona's anti-trans enacted law of the 2022-26 window is a ban on surgical care for transgender minors (2022); a 2023 governor's executive order added shield-style protections for lawful transgender health care in the state — youth-care questions are resident-facing, not visitor-facing.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment: Arizona in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC) — states that 'largely refrained from targeting transgender adults'; Arizona named alongside Virginia as having enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Prism (3 Jun 2026): Tucson Pride cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Tucson grouped with Tampa FL and Arlington TX as affected cities.

visible.summary: Highest legal floor in the country: the first sanctuary-state law for transgender care (SB 107, signed 2022) and shield protections against out-of-state enforcement. But also the most recorded incidents of any state in 2025 (198, GLAAD ALERT), a "dramatic increase" in Los Angeles hate-crime reports, and 34 recorded killings of trans women 2008–2025 (4.1 per 100k). Above the national score 0.36; law and street volume pull opposite ways.
visible.tangentialFactors: The GLAAD incident counts cover anti-LGBTQ hostility broadly (drag events, pride disruptions as well as trans-targeted abuse), and the killing rate specifically tracks trans women — volume metrics mix adjacent categories.
visible.localsOnly: SB 107's shields (medical-record privacy, bars on out-of-state investigations, arrests and cooperation around gender-affirming care) principally protect residents, patients, providers and families moving here; a short-term visitor invokes them only as a signal of official posture.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and road-safety conditions in California are ordinary travel factors affecting everyone; they do not move trans risk.

sources.claim: GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025; states with the most: California (198), New Hampshire (72), Texas (66), Ohio (50), Washington (50).

Analysis of 2025 incident data: California recorded the most incidents of any state (198), and law-enforcement data shows 'a dramatic increase' in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles during the same period as Gov. Gavin Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures.

July 2026 analysis: California falls in the 'Safest States' law band (score 4.1) with 1.9 recorded incidents - the piece argues even the most protective law floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 (September 2022), making California the first sanctuary state for transgender youth seeking care: out-of-state youth can access hormones and puberty blockers here, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care.

visible.summary:
The region contains two of the six regions with the highest recorded counts of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence in the 2012-2025 region-by-region study maintained by the country's principal LGBT monitoring project.

Against that stands the strongest judicial response to transphobic violence recorded anywhere in the country: in January 2025 a first-instance court in this region's main university city recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the association that supports trans sex workers, and - for the first time - admitted the national trans-movement organisation as civil party.

For a visitor the combination is specific: the highest-frequency regions of the country's violence record are here, but so is a documented court that named transphobic motive and ordered reparation.
visible.tangentialFactors: Rome Pride was targeted politically over the Middle East conflict (June 2025 wave) - a protest-visibility climate affecting LGBT events generally rather than a trans-specific legal mechanism.
visible.localsOnly: The Rebibbia specialized prison section and the male-prison placement policy (Rome, Lazio) concern resident detainees; they do not change a visitor's exposure beyond the national prison framework.

sources.claim: Dire news-agency report (24 Jan 2025): a Bologna first-instance court recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans (MIT) as civil party - the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in this country.

Progetto Gionata region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence 2012-2025: names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six of them ranking at the top; Lazio and Toscana (both inside Centro) are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). Provides the per-region violence distribution used to score all Italian units.

On August 30, 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato (the country's highest administrative court, seated in Rome) had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools, on the ground that the images — one showing a boy being given a red hairbow — were discriminatory and that public spaces may not be used for messages that 'generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance', particularly concerning minors. The anti-trans campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The ruling is a dated judicial outcome in the region's largest city confirming that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted there, an institutional datapoint for this region record, which otherwise centres on violence statistics and the transphobic-motive verdict in Perugia.

On March 5, 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson ('Patrizia') over the April 27, 2021 death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia, finding the death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia from accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the charge of homicide final. The case, in this region's main university city, was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant. For this record it documents that the region's courts and the highest ordinary court decided a high-profile trans-related case on the facts, complementing the record's claim about judicial responses to transphobic violence.

visible.summary:
This region hosts the country's first and second practical civic gender-recognition schemes: Milano's "registro di genere" - chosen name on civic and municipal documents, public-transport subscriptions and staff badges, created by a 2022 council motion brought by the country's first elected transgender councillor - and Torino's analogous "Identita Alias" practice at the municipality and the public libraries. For a gender-nonconforming visitor these determine whether a ticket window or municipal desk becomes an argument.

Against this, the 2012-2025 region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence names this region's two leading regions among the country's six highest-victim regions.
visible.tangentialFactors: Lombardy's 2015 regional-council motion "in support of the natural family" and against "gender ideology", and the region's rejection of WHO sexuality-education standards, are a durable political-climate signal against LGBT+ rights generally, with no visitor-facing enforcement mechanism.

sources.claim: LifeGate: Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry ('registro di genere'), letting transgender people use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents — presented as a milestone for transgender rights in the country; the record ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor, with Turin's parallel 'Identita Alias' practice at municipality and libraries.

Progetto Gionata region-and-city aggression breakdown 2012-2025: source for this record's claim that the region's two constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

visible.summary:
The state's principal international LGBT-rights federation's annual country review (February 2025) finds a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people, with incidents reported almost monthly - and includes in that finding a March 2025 scooter-mounted homophobic assault on a young man in this region's largest metropolitan periphery.

In October 2025 at a commuter railway station in the region's main metropolitan area an activist - president of a local LGBT association - was subjected to an escalating verbal homophobic attack ending in threats of stabbing by two young men. The station setting is one any visitor could occupy. The underlying local-newspaper report was bot-blocked at fetch time; it is retained as a sourced event on the strength of the recorded claim.
visible.tangentialFactors: Every documented Sud incident in the record targeted gay men rather than trans people specifically; a visitor-facing pattern of public-space homophobia that trans-presenting travellers share without being separately named.

sources.claim: International LGBT federation's annual country review for Italy (February 2025): finds a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people in 2024, incidents reported almost monthly, including the March 2025 scooter-mounted assault of a young man in Scampia (Naples).

Il Gazzettino (13 Oct 2025): Torre Annunziata — a 63-year-old man arrested after stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; a grave homophobic episode in the province of Naples, giving this record its region-specific violence datapoint.

visible.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.
visible.tangentialFactors: The July 2024 killings cluster and the lapsed bill are transfeminicide-specific, but the broader 2024 record (51 hate crimes nationally, 56.86% trans women) shows a general hostility climate toward LGBT+ people that a non-trans gender-nonconforming visitor could also meet.
visible.localsOnly: Conversion-practice criminalisation (2-5 years) on the books but unenforced, and the absence of an administrative gender-recognition procedure, are resident-facing gaps.

sources.claim: Agencia Presentes (31 Jul 2024): three trans women killed in Nuevo Leon in under a week — Arantza Castillo, 23, killed while doing sex work, and a 27 Jun motel victim still unidentified; the state justice ministry issued no case information. Nationally at least 36 trans women were transfemicided in 2024 (Asamblea Nacional Trans No Binarie); at least four in Nuevo Leon that year.

Letra S 'Las dinámicas de la violencia por prejuicio — Homicidios de personas LGBT+ en México, 2024' (May 2025): the country's longest-running civil-society hate-crime observatory (since 1998) yearbook. Records CDMX as the state with the most LGBT+ killings in 2024 (17 homicides, 11 trans women) ahead of Nuevo León (5); notes the Mexican state has no official registry of bias-motivated violence, and documents under-counting where media accounts lack victim names and gender data.

Verificado (2024): Nuevo Leon recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides during the year, and transfeminicidio is not typified in the state penal code. A labour diagnostic survey found 42.2% of the state's trans population unemployed and 35.1% discriminated against at work.

ABC Noticias (12 Jan 2026): Colectivo Casa Trans has held a planton of more than 50 days outside the Nuevo Leon congress pressing legislators to typify transfeminicidio in the state penal code; their bill was ignored for a year and lapsed, forcing a fresh filing.
